title: Algorithms at medium scale
summary: A GHZ state on 12 logical qubits in 359 physical qubits at distance 3, Deutsch–Jozsa on 13 logical qubits in 379 physical qubits at distance 3 and a GHZ state on 6 logical qubits in 419 physical qubits at distance 5, each run through the operating system's interface on a superconducting machine whose control system spans 91, 80 and 111 boards.
method: Each algorithm is a logical program. The fault-tolerant compiler lowers it to a QSysASM listing of system calls against the machine's system specification, and its resource VM admits the listing. The OS then executes every system call at its listed time on the control system, and durations the hardware needed enter the next specification until every call fits its window.

The machine is a generated superconducting chip, one transmon per RISC-Q control core, two 4-core decoders, 16,384 words of RAM per core, placed on as many AMD ZCU216 boards as it needs. Every core runs firmware compiled from the listing in the cycle-exact model of RISC-Q; boards exchange measured bits and barriers over their PutLanes.

sections.heading: The programs
sections.text: GHZ state on 12 logical qubits: 12 blocks in |+⟩ joined by a chain of Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a 12-qubit GHZ state, then read out in Z. Deutsch–Jozsa on 12 inputs: 12 inputs in |+⟩ and a target in |−⟩; a balanced oracle f(x) = s·x (s = 101101101101₂) applied as lattice-surgery CNOTs from each input of s onto the target; the inputs read out in X give s, so f is balanced. GHZ state on 6 logical qubits at distance 5: 6 blocks of the distance-5 surface code in |+⟩ joined by Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a GHZ state, then read out in Z.

findings: The largest run, GHZ state on 6 logical qubits at distance 5, uses 419 physical qubits and 428 control cores on 111 boards.
Every system call of every program ran inside its window.
The longest derivation, from compile to a specification every call fits, took 15 minutes on one workstation.
